text: A patient repeatedly demands same-day calls for nonurgent symptoms and becomes upset when limits are set. What is best?
options: Acknowledge distress, set a clear care plan and boundaries, and offer appropriate scheduled follow-up
Provide unlimited access to avoid conflict
Tell the patient they are manipulative
Ask staff to block all messages without a plan
rationale: Difficult-patient communication needs empathy plus structure. Clear expectations reduce conflict and protect care quality.

text: A patient requests an early opioid refill after losing the bottle. They are angry and in pain. What is best?
options: Acknowledge pain, assess safety and function, review the treatment agreement and records, and offer safe alternatives or reassessment
Refill automatically because the patient is upset
End the visit without assessing pain
Increase the dose to restore trust
rationale: Opioid communication should be nonjudgmental, safety-focused, and consistent. It avoids both abandonment and unsafe prescribing.

text: A patient received the wrong medication dose and required monitoring but is now stable. What should you say first?
options: I am sorry this happened. I want to explain what we know, what we are doing now, and how we will follow up.
You signed consent, so this is not our issue
We will tell you only after legal review in several months
rationale: CMPA supports open and honest communication after harm: address clinical needs, disclose known facts, express regret or apology, explain next steps, and document.

text: A resident worries that saying sorry after a medication error means admitting legal liability. What is the best teaching?
options: A sincere expression of regret and open disclosure are expected parts of patient-centred care after harm
Ask the patient to prove harm first
Let the patient discover the error from the chart
rationale: Communication after harm should be honest and compassionate. The exact legal effect of apology varies, but patient-centred disclosure remains expected.

text: Before a procedure, the patient says, "Just do whatever you think." What is best?
options: Explain the procedure, material risks, benefits, alternatives, and check understanding and voluntariness
Proceed because the patient gave blanket permission
Use the consent form as the only discussion
rationale: Consent requires information, capacity, and voluntariness. A vague statement is not enough if material information has not been discussed.

text: An older patient seems confused during consent, but they forgot hearing aids and English is not their first language. What is best?
options: Address reversible communication barriers before concluding incapacity
Ask the family to answer all questions
rationale: Capacity assessment requires communication support. Hearing, language, delirium, pain, anxiety, and medications may affect performance.

text: A capable patient refuses admission for pneumonia after understanding risks. What is the best communication response?
options: Respect the decision, explore reasons, offer alternatives, safety-net, and document informed refusal
Tell the family to override the patient
rationale: A capable patient may refuse recommended care. Good communication explores values and barriers, offers safer alternatives, and documents.

text: A frail patient with advanced COPD asks, "Am I dying?" The family says not to discuss it. What is best?
options: Ask what the patient understands and wants to know, answer honestly and compassionately, and discuss goals of care
Avoid the question because the family objected
Say everyone dies eventually and move on
rationale: End-of-life communication should be honest, patient-led, and values-focused. Families can be included with patient permission.

text: A patient with metastatic cancer is admitted. Which question best begins a goals-of-care conversation?
options: What do you understand about your illness, and what matters most to you if your health worsens?
Do you want us to do everything?
You do not want CPR, right?
Your family should decide your code status
rationale: Goals-of-care discussions should explore understanding, values, acceptable outcomes, and then connect recommendations to those values.

text: A patient’s spouse died last week. They cry during the visit and say they feel lost. What is best?
options: Offer condolences, allow emotion, ask about supports and safety, and arrange follow-up
Prescribe sedatives immediately to stop crying
Say they should be over it soon
Tell them grief is not medical
rationale: Grief communication requires presence, validation, assessment of supports and safety, and follow-up. Pathology is considered when symptoms are severe, persistent, or dangerous.

text: A family says their hospitalized parent suddenly became confused and asks if this is dementia. What is best?
options: Explain that sudden fluctuating confusion suggests delirium, look for causes, and involve them in reorientation and safety
Say it is definitely permanent dementia
Ignore the family because they are not the patient
Use restraints as the first explanation
rationale: Communication with family can help identify baseline cognition and support non-drug delirium care. Avoid premature labels.

text: A patient with dementia becomes angry when told driving safety must be addressed. What is best?
options: Acknowledge the loss, explain the safety and legal duty, discuss alternatives, and report when required
Avoid the topic to preserve the relationship
Let the family hide the keys without discussion only
Say angry patients cannot be counselled
Promise not to report if they drive less
rationale: Driving conversations require empathy plus public safety. Losing a licence affects identity and independence, so discuss alternatives.

text: An older patient appears fearful of a caregiver and has unexplained bruises. What is best?
options: Speak with the patient alone if safe, ask directly and gently about mistreatment, assess capacity and immediate safety
Ask the caregiver to explain everything in front of the patient
Ignore it if the caregiver seems nice
rationale: Elder abuse communication requires privacy, safety, capacity assessment, and knowledge of reporting obligations.

text: A patient demands that you write they are permanently unable to work, but your assessment does not support this. What is best?
options: Explain you can document findings and functional limits accurately, but cannot exaggerate or certify unsupported claims
Write what they request to avoid conflict
Document only the patient’s opinion as your conclusion
rationale: Forms are professional communication. They should be accurate, objective, and based on assessment.

text: A patient asks for HIV results by voicemail on a shared family phone. What is best?
options: Use a privacy-protecting method, verify identity, and agree on how sensitive results will be communicated
Leave the full result because the patient requested voicemail
Post the result on social media
Refuse to give any results ever by phone
rationale: Sensitive result communication needs privacy, identity verification, and patient preference balanced with confidentiality.

text: During a video visit, the patient is in a car with other people present and wants to discuss STI symptoms. What is best?
options: Confirm identity, location, privacy, and whether they want to continue before sensitive discussion
Proceed because video visits are always private
rationale: Virtual care needs privacy checks, location for emergencies, identity confirmation, and consent to continue.

text: A patient with diabetes is not taking medication because it is too expensive and feels embarrassed. What is best?
options: Ask about affordability in a nonjudgmental way and choose an effective affordable plan together
Tell them nonadherence is their fault
Prescribe the newest drug without discussing cost
Stop all treatment because they cannot pay
Ask only the insurer, not the patient
rationale: Cost is a clinical barrier. Asking directly and respectfully can improve adherence and equity.

text: A patient with heart failure cannot describe how to adjust diuretics and has been readmitted twice. What is best?
options: Use plain language, written instructions, teach-back, and involve supports with consent
Repeat the same technical explanation louder
rationale: Health literacy communication uses plain language, chunking, written plans, and teach-back.

text: A patient says a 30% relative risk reduction sounds huge. What is best?
options: Explain the baseline risk and absolute risk reduction using natural frequencies when possible
Agree that relative risk is enough
Use statistics to pressure the patient
Say the patient is bad at math
rationale: Natural frequencies and absolute risk help patients understand benefit and harm. This supports informed consent.

text: A patient brings printed online information about a supplement and asks your opinion. What is best?
options: Review it respectfully, discuss source quality, benefits, harms, interactions, and the patient’s goals
Dismiss it because it came from the internet
Tell them not to read health information
Replace all prescribed drugs with the supplement
rationale: Respectful discussion of online information builds trust and allows harm reduction. Source quality and patient goals matter.

text: A patient brings an AI-generated diagnosis and says it proves they need antibiotics. What is best?
options: Acknowledge the concern, explain that AI is not a diagnosis, assess clinically, and use reliable sources for the decision
Prescribe because AI is usually right
Document the AI output as the diagnosis
Tell the patient AI is illegal
rationale: AI output can be discussed, but clinical responsibility remains with the clinician. Communication should be respectful and evidence-based.

text: A nurse raises concern that a medication order seems unsafe. What is the best response?
options: Thank them, review the order together, clarify the concern, and correct it if needed
Tell them not to question physicians
Ignore the concern unless the patient complains
rationale: Good team communication improves safety. Hierarchy should not block concern escalation.

text: You are handing over a patient with sepsis risk to the night team. What is best?
options: Use a structured handoff with diagnosis, current status, pending tests, contingency plan, and what to do if worse
Say the patient is complicated and leave
Assume the team will read every note
rationale: Handoffs need clear structure and contingency planning. Communication failure can cause harm.

text: A patient’s abnormal potassium result returns after the visit. What communication plan is best?
options: Ensure timely review, contact the patient with clear instructions, document the action, and arrange urgent care if needed
Assume no news is good news
Wait until the next annual checkup
Ask the patient to interpret the portal result alone
Delete the result if the patient is hard to reach
rationale: Result management requires clear communication, responsibility, documentation, and escalation for dangerous findings.

text: A patient is angry that a specialist appointment will take months. What is best?
options: Explain the triage process, review red flags, optimize current care, and update urgency if the condition changes
Say there is nothing you can do and end the visit
Tell the patient to exaggerate symptoms
rationale: Communication around waiting lists should be honest and clinically active. Urgency should match need, not pressure.

text: A patient asks for treatment for a minor ailment, but the history includes red flags. What is best communication?
options: Explain the red flags in plain language and why referral or urgent assessment is safer than self-care only
Treat as minor because the patient requested it
rationale: Minor ailment communication must explain why a presentation is not minor when red flags are present.

text: A pregnant patient asks whether they must do prenatal genetic screening. What is best?
options: Explain the purpose, options, benefits, limits, possible outcomes, and support the patient’s informed choice
Say all pregnant patients must be screened
rationale: Prenatal screening is preference-sensitive. Communication should support informed consent and values.

text: A patient has an early pregnancy loss and asks if it was caused by something they did. What is best?
options: Use compassionate language, avoid blame, explain that most early losses are not caused by routine activity, and offer follow-up
Avoid answering because it is emotional
Say at least it was early
rationale: Pregnancy-loss communication should avoid blame, validate grief, answer questions, and provide follow-up and safety information.

text: A patient asks for contraception but worries about side effects and future fertility. What is best?
options: Ask priorities, explain effective options and side effects, correct myths, and support the patient’s choice
Choose the most effective method without discussion
Provide no contraception until the patient is certain forever
rationale: Contraception counselling is values-based. Effectiveness, side effects, contraindications, reversibility, access, and patient preference matter.

text: A patient with gonorrhea is embarrassed and refuses to tell partners. What is best?
options: Explain reinfection and partner health, discuss confidential notification options, and follow public health requirements
Shame the patient until they agree
Ignore partners because the patient was treated
rationale: STI communication should reduce shame, protect confidentiality, and support partner notification and treatment through appropriate pathways.

text: A teen with weight loss says, "Do not tell my parents." Vitals are concerning. What is best?
options: Explain confidentiality limits, assess safety and capacity, involve guardians or urgent care when medically necessary
Delay all care until they agree
rationale: Communication must balance confidentiality with safety. Serious medical instability may require urgent intervention and appropriate involvement.

text: A patient with persecutory delusions says cameras are watching them. What is best?
options: Do not argue about the belief. Acknowledge distress, assess risk, and focus on safety and treatment
Tell them the belief is stupid
Ask family to restrain them at home
rationale: Psychosis communication should avoid validating delusions or arguing. The clinician validates distress and assesses safety.

text: A manic patient speaks rapidly, interrupts, and tries to leave before risk assessment. What is best?
options: Use calm concise statements, reduce stimulation, assess safety and capacity, and involve urgent psychiatric care when needed
Let them leave without assessing risk
Ask other patients to help calm them
rationale: Mania communication works best with calm, brief, structured interaction while assessing risk, capacity, and need for urgent care.

text: A patient says, “I do not want to be dependent on antidepressants. I want to quit today.” Which response is best?
options: “You are wrong. These medications are not addictive, so keep taking them.”
“I hear that you want to stop. Let us review why you want to stop, your relapse risk, and make a safe taper plan together.”
“Stop today and call only if symptoms become unbearable.”
“I cannot discuss stopping medication because it is against guidelines.”
“If you stop, you will definitely relapse.”
rationale: The best communication answer validates the concern, avoids arguing, explains risk, and invites shared planning. This is both communication and management. The exam often rewards the sentence that keeps the patient engaged while protecting safety.

text: A patient says, “This clinic does not care. I waited two hours and nobody listened.” Vitals are stable. What is the best first response?
options: I can see this has been frustrating, and I want to understand what worries you most right now
The schedule is not my responsibility
If you are angry, I cannot help you
You should book somewhere else next time
We need to finish quickly because other patients are waiting
rationale: The first response should acknowledge emotion and invite the patient concern before moving to diagnosis or treatment. This is a common MCCQE1 communication trap.

text: A patient with viral upper respiratory symptoms insists on antibiotics because they have a job interview in two days. What is the best response?
options: I understand why you want to recover quickly. Antibiotics would not help a viral infection and can cause harm; let us focus on symptom relief and warning signs
Take antibiotics so you can return to work faster
There is nothing to do for viral infections
You are wrong to ask for antibiotics
I will order a chest CT to prove it is viral
rationale: The best answer combines empathy, explanation of benefit and harm, symptom care, and safety-netting. It avoids unsafe prescribing and avoids dismissing the patient.

sub: Opioid refill request with safety concern
text: A patient becomes upset when an early opioid refill is declined. What is the best communication approach?
options: I can see you are in pain. I cannot safely refill early today, but I will reassess your pain, withdrawal risk, function, and make a safe plan with you
I will refill it if you promise this is the last time
You have addiction, so I cannot treat you
Call another physician for the refill
rationale: MCCQE1 favours non-abandonment, validation, reassessment, safety, and boundaries. The answer should not escalate dose just to end conflict.

text: A CT scan strongly suggests metastatic cancer. The patient asks, “Is it bad?” What should the physician say next?
options: I am afraid the scan shows something serious, and I would like to go through it with you step by step
You have metastatic cancer and little time left
Let us wait until oncology because I cannot discuss this
Your family asked me not to tell you
At least we found it early
rationale: Bad news should start with a warning shot, then small pieces of information, pauses for emotion, and follow-up.

text: Family members ask the physician not to tell a capable patient about a new cancer diagnosis. The patient previously said they want all information. What is best?
options: Explore the family’s concern, then speak with the patient according to the patient’s expressed wish for information
Follow the family request because they know the patient best
Document that the diagnosis is confidential from the patient
Tell the patient only if the family leaves the room
Ask the family to sign consent for treatment
rationale: A capable patient controls their own information. The physician can support the family, but should not deceive a patient who wants to know.

text: A patient with limited English nods during a surgical consent discussion while the adult child translates. What is the safest next step?
options: Arrange a qualified medical interpreter and confirm understanding with teach-back
Accept the child’s translation because the patient nodded
Proceed because the consent form is signed
Ask the child to decide for the patient
rationale: Consent requires understanding. Family interpreters may create errors, omissions, confidentiality issues, or pressure.

text: An older patient starts insulin and says the instructions are clear, but looks confused. What should the clinician say?
options: Just so I can check I explained it clearly, can you show me how you will take it at home?
Read the pamphlet when you get home
Your family will figure it out
This is simple, so you should understand it
Come back only if something goes wrong
rationale: Teach-back checks the clinician’s explanation, not the patient’s intelligence. It improves safety for medications and discharge plans.

text: A patient says they were sexually assaulted last night and begins crying. What is the best first response?
options: I am sorry this happened. You are safe here. We can go at your pace and discuss medical care, evidence options, and support
You must report this to police now
I need all details before I can help
Try not to think about it
rationale: The best response is trauma-informed, validates the patient, supports choice, and avoids blame or forced reporting unless a mandatory reporting situation applies.

text: A patient discloses partner violence but says they are not ready to leave. What is the best response?
options: Validate the disclosure, assess immediate safety, discuss a safety plan and resources, and respect the patient’s pace unless mandatory reporting applies
Tell the patient to leave today or you cannot help
Call the partner into the room to discuss it
Document nothing because it is private
Prescribe sedatives to reduce conflict at home
rationale: IPV questions test safety planning and patient autonomy. Leaving can increase risk. The clinician should assess danger and connect supports.

text: A depressed patient says, “Everyone would be better without me.” What should the physician ask?
options: Are you thinking about killing yourself?
You do not really mean that, right?
You should focus on positive thoughts
Can we talk about sleep instead?
Promise me you will not do anything
rationale: MCCQE1 expects direct, clear suicide assessment. Asking does not implant the idea.

text: A patient was given the wrong medication dose but is now clinically stable. What is the best communication step?
options: Explain the known facts, express regret, describe current care and monitoring, and arrange follow-up
Wait until the internal review is complete before saying anything
Tell the patient a nurse caused the problem
Alter the chart to avoid confusion
Only disclose if permanent harm occurs
rationale: Disclosure should be timely, factual, compassionate, and documented. Avoid speculation or blame while analysis is incomplete.

text: The team knows harm occurred, but the cause is still under review. What should be said?
options: We know what happened clinically, we are still reviewing why it happened, and we will update you as we learn more
We cannot talk until lawyers finish
rationale: When cause is uncertain, communicate known facts, current care, and follow-up. Do not speculate.

text: A patient brings an AI-generated report saying they likely have cancer and demands urgent full-body MRI. What is best?
options: Explore the concern, review symptoms and risk, explain the limits of the AI output, and choose evidence-based next steps
Dismiss the report without reading it
Order full-body MRI to reassure the patient
Tell the patient AI is always wrong
rationale: The best response respects the concern but does not follow low-value testing. It uses shared decision-making and appropriate screening or diagnostic pathways.

text: A patient with acute mechanical low back pain and no red flags asks for MRI. What is the best explanation?
options: MRI is not likely to help at this stage and can find incidental changes that lead to harm; let us treat symptoms and review red flags
I will order MRI because you asked
Only specialists can examine back pain
rationale: Choosing Wisely-style communication explains why not testing is safer, gives an active plan, and safety-nets red flags.

text: A parent is worried vaccines may overwhelm the immune system. What is the best response?
options: Ask what they have heard, acknowledge the concern, explain benefits and risks clearly, and keep the conversation open
Refuse future care unless they vaccinate today
rationale: Motivational communication starts with listening, then clear recommendation and risk explanation. Shaming usually worsens resistance.

text: A patient with COPD smokes daily and says they are not ready to quit. What is the best response?
options: Ask permission to discuss smoking, explore goals, offer help when ready, and arrange follow-up
Lecture about death risk for the rest of the visit
rationale: Behaviour-change questions often test readiness, permission, brief advice, support, and follow-up.

text: A patient with aphasia appears unable to answer complex questions about treatment. What is the best next step?
options: Use communication supports and assess understanding and appreciation for this decision
Ask the family to decide before assessment
rationale: Capacity assessment requires support for communication. Speech or language impairment alone does not prove incapacity.

text: A 15-year-old asks for contraception and does not want parents told. What should the physician explain first?
options: I will assess your capacity and keep your care confidential unless there is a serious safety concern or legal reporting duty
I must tell your parents everything
I cannot see minors without parents
Contraception is illegal without parental consent
rationale: Mature minor questions test capacity, confidentiality, and limits such as safety or mandatory reporting.

text: A patient is unsure about a screening test with modest benefit and possible false positives. What is best?
options: Explain absolute benefits and harms, ask what matters to the patient, and decide together
Tell the patient guidelines remove the need for discussion
rationale: Shared decision-making uses clear absolute risk, benefits, harms, uncertainty, and patient values.

text: A patient with advanced illness asks, “Am I dying?” What is the best response?
options: I worry time may be limited. Can we talk about what matters most to you if things get worse?
No one can know, so do not ask
We should continue every treatment until the end
rationale: Goals-of-care communication should be honest, gentle, and linked to patient values and planning.

text: A patient with cognitive decline becomes angry when driving risk is raised. What is best?
options: I know driving is important to your independence. My role is to assess safety, discuss risks, and follow the reporting rules that apply here
You are old, so you cannot drive
I will ignore it if you promise to be careful
I will report you without explaining why
rationale: Driving questions test respectful counselling, safety, documentation, and jurisdiction-specific reporting.

text: A patient stopped an antidepressant suddenly because of nausea and now has dizziness and electric-shock sensations. What is best?
options: Explain these can occur after abrupt stopping, assess safety and relapse symptoms, and discuss restarting or tapering with follow-up
Tell the patient antidepressants are addictive and should never be used
Ignore symptoms because they are psychological
Restart at double dose without assessment
rationale: This tests counselling plus management sequence. Abrupt discontinuation can cause symptoms; assess risk, explain, and taper when appropriate.

text: At the end of a visit, a patient says, “One more thing, I had chest pressure yesterday.” What is best?
options: Take the symptom seriously, assess immediate risk, and arrange urgent evaluation if indicated
Say there is no time and leave
Book a routine visit next month without questions
Tell the patient to search symptoms online
rationale: Communication questions still require clinical safety. A late concern with red flags needs triage, not dismissal.

text: An Indigenous patient says they avoid the hospital because of prior racist treatment. What is the best response?
options: Thank them for telling you, acknowledge the harm, ask what would make care safer today, and offer supports
Defend the hospital because staff try hard
Tell them all patients are treated the same
Ask them to prove what happened
rationale: Cultural safety requires acknowledging the patient’s experience and adapting care to reduce harm.

text: A patient says they cannot afford the prescribed medication. What is the best response?
options: Thank them for telling you, explore coverage and lower-cost options, and choose an affordable evidence-based plan
Tell them health is more important than money
Prescribe the same drug and hope they buy it
rationale: Cost-sensitive prescribing is patient-centred and prevents nonadherence. It is also an equity issue.

text: A patient asks for a work note stating they were unable to work for a month, but you only assessed them today. What is best?
options: Explain you can document what you assessed today and any information you can verify, but cannot certify facts you do not know
Write the note to preserve rapport
Backdate the note if the patient seems honest
Ask the employer what they want written
rationale: Professional communication includes honesty in documentation while still helping within the evidence available.

text: Before a pelvic examination, what is the best communication step?
options: Explain the reason and steps, ask for consent, offer a chaperone according to policy, and remind the patient they can ask to stop
Ask consent only after the exam
Tell the patient refusal cancels all care
Let family consent for an adult patient
rationale: Sensitive exams require explanation, consent, dignity, and ability to stop.

text: A patient with opioid use disorder misses appointments and asks for help. What is best?
options: Use nonjudgmental language, reassess safety and goals, and offer evidence-based treatment and follow-up
rationale: MCCQE1 favours non-stigmatizing language, harm reduction, and continuity.

text: A patient is anxious about a mildly abnormal lab result with low clinical concern. What is best?
options: Acknowledge the worry, explain what the result means in context, and give a clear follow-up plan
Say it is normal and move on
Order every possible test for reassurance
Tell the patient anxiety is the real problem
Avoid numbers because they confuse patients
rationale: Good counselling explains context and next steps while avoiding overtesting.

text: A child with likely viral gastroenteritis is well hydrated and going home. What instruction is best?
options: Explain fluids, expected course, and specific return signs such as lethargy, blood in stool, persistent vomiting, dehydration, or worsening symptoms
Say return if concerned without details
rationale: Safety-netting should be specific, concrete, and linked to red flags.

text: An incapable patient needs non-urgent treatment and has no advance directive. Two relatives disagree about who may decide. What should the physician do?
options: Follow the applicable provincial substitute decision-maker hierarchy and seek the legally authorized decision-maker
Choose the relative who agrees with the physician
rationale: When the patient lacks capacity, consent comes from the authorized substitute decision-maker according to jurisdictional law.

text: A substitute decision-maker asks for treatment that the team believes is outside the patient’s values and interests. What is best?
options: Clarify the patient’s prior wishes and values, explain medical options, and use the conflict-resolution process if disagreement remains
Ignore the substitute and proceed secretly
Ask the hospital lawyer to decide at the bedside
rationale: Substitute decisions should reflect prior capable wishes or best interests, not the substitute’s personal preference.

text: A mandatory report is required for a safety issue. What privacy principle still applies?
options: Disclose only the information necessary to the appropriate authority and document the reason
Send the entire lifetime chart automatically
Tell the patient’s employer as a courtesy
Post the concern in the team chat broadly
rationale: Even when disclosure is allowed or required, it should be limited to what is needed for the purpose.

text: A physician starts a virtual visit and learns the patient is currently in another province. What is best?
options: Confirm the patient’s location, assess urgency, and follow applicable licensing, privacy, and emergency-care requirements
Tell the patient to pretend they are local
End the call even if there is an emergency
rationale: Virtual care requires knowing where the patient is for emergency response, privacy, and jurisdictional obligations.

text: A patient offers an expensive gift after a successful treatment. What is the best response?
options: Thank the patient, decline or manage according to professional policy, and preserve boundaries
Ask for a larger gift to donate
rationale: Professional boundaries protect trust and avoid conflicts of interest.

text: A patient sends a friend request and a clinical question through personal social media. What is best?
options: Maintain boundaries and redirect clinical communication to appropriate secure channels
Accept the request to improve rapport
rationale: Clinical communication should occur through appropriate channels that protect privacy, documentation, and boundaries.

text: A patient feels pressured to join a study because their treating physician is recruiting them. What is most important?
options: Make voluntariness clear and reassure that refusal will not affect clinical care
Explain that research is mandatory when treatment options are limited
Hide the risks to improve enrollment
rationale: Research consent must be voluntary and separate from pressure in the therapeutic relationship.

text: A physician recommends a private clinic in which they have a financial interest. What is required?
options: Disclose the conflict, offer reasonable alternatives, and ensure the patient can choose freely
Do not mention the interest unless asked
Say the clinic is the only option
Ask the patient to sign a confidentiality agreement
rationale: Conflicts should be disclosed and managed so patient choice is informed and free from pressure.

text: A clinician has reasonable grounds to suspect a child may need protection. What is the best next step?
options: Report promptly to the designated child protection authority according to local law
Ask the suspected caregiver for permission
rationale: Child protection reporting is based on reasonable suspicion, not proof. Investigation belongs to child protection authorities.

text: A patient states a clear, imminent plan to seriously harm an identifiable person. What is best?
options: Take protective action with limited necessary disclosure and document the rationale
Disclose the whole chart to the media
rationale: A serious imminent risk to an identifiable person can justify protective disclosure. The disclosure should be limited and documented.

text: A patient with advanced illness asks about MAID. What is the best first response?
options: Explore the reason for the request, assess suffering and supports, provide information, and follow the legal eligibility and referral process
Refuse to discuss it because it is illegal
Approve immediately because the patient requested it
Call psychiatry for every request before listening
Tell the family before speaking with the patient
rationale: MAID questions require respectful exploration, assessment of suffering, capacity and eligibility, and following legal process.

text: An incapable patient has a clear prior directive refusing intubation, but family asks for intubation now. What is best?
options: Follow the valid prior capable wish if applicable, while explaining and supporting the family
Ignore the directive because family is present
Ask the family to rewrite it
Let the most senior physician decide by preference
rationale: Prior capable wishes guide substitute decisions when applicable. Family distress should be supported but does not erase the patient’s values.

text: A patient asks the physician to write that they have a diagnosis that was never assessed to obtain insurance coverage. What is best?
options: Decline to certify inaccurate information and offer to document verified clinical facts
Write it because it helps the patient
Ask the patient what wording insurer prefers
rationale: Medical documentation must be truthful, accurate, and based on clinical assessment.

text: A medical learner will perform part of a procedure. What should occur?
options: The patient should know the learner’s role and consent to their involvement according to the care context
Learner status should be hidden to reduce anxiety
Consent is unnecessary because learners need experience
Only the supervisor’s consent is needed
The learner should proceed if the patient is sedated
rationale: Patients should receive accurate information about who is involved in their care, especially procedures, and consent should be respected.

text: Two patients need one scarce resource and have similar urgency. What principle is most defensible?
options: Use transparent, consistent, clinically relevant criteria through the established process
Let the clinician secretly choose the nicer patient
rationale: Scarce resources should be allocated with fair, transparent and clinically relevant criteria, not social worth.

text: A 47-year-old with schizophrenia refuses an elective operation. They accurately explain the diagnosis, the proposed operation, the important alternatives, and the likely consequences of declining it. Their decision differs from the surgical team’s recommendation. What is the best next step?
options: Respect the informed refusal, document the capacity assessment and discussion, and offer reasonable alternatives
Declare the patient incapable because schizophrenia is present
Ask the family to consent because the decision appears unwise
Proceed with the operation because it offers the best medical outcome
Postpone all care until the patient agrees with the team
rationale: Capacity is specific to the decision and the time. A capable person understands the nature and anticipated effects of the treatment and alternatives, and appreciates the consequences of refusal. A diagnosis or an unwise choice does not by itself establish incapacity.

text: A capable patient is brought to the emergency department by police after a motor vehicle collision. A police officer asks the physician to collect a blood sample. The patient asks whether they must agree. No court order, warrant, or statutory authority has been provided. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Explain the proposed collection and obtain voluntary, informed consent; a police request alone is not a substitute for consent or lawful authority
Collect the sample because police presence makes the consent voluntary
Sedate the patient and collect the sample before they can refuse
Ask a relative to consent for this capable adult
Collect the sample and discuss consent only if the result is positive
rationale: Valid consent must be voluntary, informed, and given by a person with capacity. Police involvement can create pressure, so the clinician should ensure the patient understands the proposed intervention and that a police request is not treated as consent. Legal authority can change the situation, but it must be established rather than assumed.

text: A 15-year-old in Alberta seeks treatment for a sensitive health concern. They demonstrate a clear understanding of the treatment, alternatives, expected effects, and consequences of refusing. What principle should guide consent?
options: Assess capacity case by case; in most of Canada, age alone does not decide whether a minor can consent
Refuse care until a parent attends because all people under 18 lack capacity
Require parental consent because the concern is sensitive
Assume capacity only after the age of majority
Disclose the visit to family before assessing the young person
rationale: In most Canadian provinces and territories, a minor’s ability to consent depends on capacity rather than age alone. The clinician should assess whether the young person can understand and appreciate the proposed care and its consequences, while applying applicable provincial rules and mandatory-reporting obligations.

text: An 11-year-old cannot explain the purpose, alternatives, or likely consequences of a proposed non-emergency procedure. A parent with decision-making responsibility is present. What is the most appropriate consent approach?
options: Obtain consent from the authorized parent or guardian, guided by the child’s best interests, and involve the child as much as possible
Treat the child as capable because they can state a preference
Proceed without any consent because a parent is present
Ask any accompanying adult to sign the consent
Delay indefinitely because minors can never receive elective care
rationale: When a minor lacks the capacity to consent, the authorized parent or guardian generally provides consent, guided by the child’s best interests. The child should still receive an age-appropriate explanation and be involved whenever possible.

text: A capable adult’s parent calls the clinic and asks whether the patient attended an appointment and what was discussed. The patient has not consented to any disclosure. What is the best response?
options: Maintain confidentiality and do not disclose information without the patient’s consent or a valid exception
Provide a short summary because the caller is family
Confirm the appointment but withhold only the diagnosis
Send the parent a copy of the chart after verifying identity
Discuss the case if the parent promises not to tell anyone
rationale: Confidentiality applies to the fact of a clinical relationship as well as to diagnosis and treatment details. Family relationship alone does not create authority to receive information about a capable adult.

text: Police ask an emergency physician to provide a patient’s medical record after an assault. The patient is capable, refuses consent, and no legal authority requiring disclosure has been presented. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Refrain from disclosure unless consent is obtained or a legal exception or authority is established
Give the record because the investigation involves a serious offence
Give only the laboratory results without consent
Ask police to obtain family permission instead
Discuss the record verbally because it is not a written disclosure
rationale: Physicians generally should not disclose patient information to police or another third party without patient consent unless disclosure is permitted or required by law. The correct action is to identify the applicable authority rather than assume that an investigation overrides confidentiality.

text: A clinician has reasonable grounds to suspect that a child is being physically abused. The caregiver asks the clinician not to contact child protective services. What is the best next step?
options: Make the required report to child protective services and disclose only information relevant to the concern
Wait until abuse is proven beyond doubt
Tell a neighbour instead of the proper reporting authority
Keep the concern confidential because the child did not ask for help
rationale: All provinces and territories require reporting when there are reasonable grounds to believe or suspect that a child has been abused or is at risk of abuse. The report should include only the facts and circumstances necessary for the concern.

text: A physician identifies a possible duty to report a patient’s fitness to drive. The exact requirement differs by province. Which approach is best?
options: Review the applicable provincial law and College guidance, act on reasonable grounds in good faith, and document the rationale, recipient, and information disclosed
Always disclose the entire medical record to the licensing authority
Never report unless the patient agrees
Make an anonymous social-media post about the concern
Ignore the concern because reporting rules differ between provinces
rationale: A duty to report can be mandatory or discretionary, depending on the governing statute, regulation, by-law, or policy. The clinician should identify the applicable rule, disclose only what is necessary, and document the reasoning and details of any report.

text: A medication administration error caused symptomatic hypoglycemia, which was promptly treated without lasting harm. The patient is now stable. What is the most appropriate communication plan?
options: Provide necessary care and disclose the poor clinical outcome openly and honestly as soon as reasonably possible, including known facts and the follow-up plan
Wait to disclose until a complaint is filed
Avoid discussing the event because the patient recovered
Change the chart so the event is less visible
Ask another clinician to disclose without first addressing the patient’s care
rationale: Healthcare providers have ethical, professional, and legal obligations to communicate openly about harm from healthcare delivery. The patient’s immediate clinical needs come first, followed by timely, factual communication and appropriate follow-up.

text: A statute requires a clinician to report a defined communicable disease. Which confidentiality principle best applies to the report?
options: Disclose only the information necessary to fulfill the legal reporting obligation and document the disclosure
Send the full lifetime chart to make the report more complete
Avoid reporting because confidentiality is always absolute
Tell unrelated family members before reporting
Post the diagnosis publicly so contacts can identify themselves
rationale: When disclosure is required or permitted, confidentiality is not abandoned. The information released should be limited to what strictly fulfills the legal purpose, and the clinician should document why and how disclosure occurred.

text: A 58-year-old agrees to a colonoscopy after being told only that it is a routine test. The physician does not discuss material risks, benefits, or reasonable alternatives. Which element of valid consent is most clearly missing?
options: Proper information for an informed decision
A written consent form in every circumstance
rationale: Valid consent requires that the patient has capacity, acts voluntarily, and receives the information a reasonable person in that situation would need, including material risks, benefits, and alternatives.

text: A patient with bipolar disorder refuses lithium because they worry about renal effects. They explain the diagnosis, benefits, alternatives, and consequences of refusal. What is the best next step?
options: Respect the refusal and document the capacity and informed refusal discussion
Declare incapacity because bipolar disorder is present
Ask the family to override the refusal
Admit involuntarily for medication administration only
Proceed because the medication is guideline-supported
rationale: Capacity is assessed for the specific decision at the specific time. A psychiatric diagnosis or a decision the physician disagrees with does not prove incapacity.

text: An unconscious trauma patient has life-threatening hemorrhage. No substitute decision-maker is available, and there is no known prior refusal. What should the physician do?
options: Provide immediately necessary care and document why consent could not be obtained
Wait until a family member arrives
Provide no care because consent is absent
Ask another patient to witness consent
rationale: In an emergency with imminent threat to life or health, care that is immediately necessary may proceed when consent cannot be obtained. Known prior wishes should still be respected, and consent should be obtained as soon as reasonably possible.

text: An older adult lacks capacity for a high-risk operation. A neighbour says they know what the patient would want, but no legal authority is shown. What is the best approach?
options: Identify the legally authorized substitute decision-maker under the applicable jurisdiction before obtaining consent
Accept the neighbour's consent because they sound confident
Ask the surgeon to sign for the patient
Proceed because the operation is high risk
rationale: When a patient lacks capacity, consent must come from the legally authorized substitute decision-maker or another valid legal source, depending on provincial or territorial law.

text: A patient completed advance care planning two years ago. They are now capable and request a treatment that conflicts with the old written plan. Which principle is best?
options: Follow the current capable patient's decision
Follow the older document even though the patient is capable
Ask the family to decide instead
Treat advance care planning as consent to every future intervention
Ignore both the patient and the document
rationale: Advance care planning helps guide future decisions if capacity is lost. It does not replace the consent of a currently capable patient for a specific treatment decision.

text: An incapable patient previously discussed medical assistance in dying with family, but no valid waiver arrangement applies. The substitute decision-maker asks the physician to proceed with MAID. What is the best response?
options: Do not proceed based on substitute decision-maker consent
Proceed if two family members sign
Treat MAID like any routine medication consent
Ask the hospital lawyer to sign consent
rationale: CMPA guidance notes that a substitute decision-maker cannot consent to MAID on behalf of an incapable patient. MAID has specific eligibility and safeguard requirements.

text: A capable adult's spouse calls the clinic asking for the patient's HIV test result. The patient has not consented to disclosure. What is the best response?
options: Do not disclose without consent or a valid legal exception
Disclose because spouses are inside confidentiality
Confirm only whether the test was positive
Send the result by text to avoid a phone discussion
Ask the spouse to promise confidentiality
rationale: Confidentiality protects personal health information and the fact of care. Family relationship alone does not authorize disclosure for a capable adult.

text: A hospital consultant needs relevant medication history to manage an admitted patient. The consultant is directly involved in the patient's care. Which confidentiality principle applies?
options: Share relevant information within the circle of care when needed for care
Withhold all information unless a new written consent is signed for every clinician
Share the entire record with all hospital staff
Discuss the case in a public elevator
Post a de-identified story with enough details for colleagues to recognize the patient
rationale: Relevant information may be shared within the care team for patient care. Disclosure should still be limited to what is needed and handled in a private, professional way.

text: Police ask an emergency physician for a patient's chart after an assault. The patient is capable and refuses. Police provide no warrant, subpoena, court order, or statutory authority. What is the best response?
options: Decline disclosure unless consent or valid legal authority is obtained
Give the chart because the offence is serious
Give a verbal summary because it is not written
Ask a nurse to disclose instead
Disclose only abnormal results without consent
rationale: Physicians should generally avoid disclosing patient information to police or other third parties without consent unless a legal exception or authority applies.

text: A physician has reasonable grounds to suspect a child is being neglected. The parent asks the physician to wait until there is proof. What should the physician do?
options: Report promptly to the child protection authority according to local law
Wait for proof beyond a reasonable doubt
Ask the parent to decide whether to report
Document only and take no action
Tell the school but not child protection
rationale: Canadian provinces and territories require reporting when there are reasonable grounds to believe or suspect that a child has been abused, neglected, or is at risk.

text: A child protection worker asks for information after a required report. What information should the physician provide?
options: Facts and circumstances necessary for the report and child protection concern
Unrelated mental health records of all relatives
Only the child's name with no clinical facts
Public social media posts about the case
rationale: Even when reporting is required, disclosure should be limited to information necessary to make the report and address the protection concern.

text: A clinician thinks a patient may meet a mandatory reporting rule. The rule differs across provinces and territories. What is the best first step?
options: Check the applicable provincial or territorial law and College guidance
Use Ontario rules everywhere in Canada
Always report the entire chart to every regulator
Ignore the concern because rules differ
rationale: Reporting duties may arise from statute, regulation, by-law, or policy and can be mandatory or discretionary. The physician should identify the applicable local requirement.

text: A patient has recurrent unexplained loss of consciousness and continues to drive. What is the best physician approach?
options: Assess risk, counsel the patient not to drive, document, and follow the applicable reporting law
Ignore driving because it is a licensing issue only
Report the full chart to the employer
Tell the family to hide the car keys and do nothing else
rationale: Medical fitness-to-drive reporting rules differ by province and territory, but patient and public safety require assessment, counselling, documentation, and compliance with local law.

text: A patient describes a specific plan to seriously harm an identifiable person today. Which confidentiality principle is most appropriate?
options: Consider protective disclosure limited to what is necessary to reduce the serious imminent risk
Disclose the whole record to the public
Wait until the person is harmed
Only document and take no action
rationale: A serious public-safety risk can justify limited disclosure without consent. The disclosure should be directed to the appropriate party and limited to the information needed to reduce the risk.

text: A patient receives the wrong medication dose and develops symptomatic hypotension. The team treats the patient and the patient stabilizes. What should happen next?
options: Disclose the known facts, express concern, explain current care and follow-up, and document
Do not disclose because the patient stabilized
Change the record to avoid confusion
Blame one staff member before review is complete
Wait until the patient files a complaint
rationale: Open and honest communication after harm should occur as soon as reasonably possible after immediate clinical needs are addressed. Early disclosure should focus on known facts, care, and follow-up.

text: A patient is harmed during care, but the team does not yet know why it happened. What should the physician say in the first disclosure discussion?
options: Share what is known, avoid speculation or blame, and commit to follow-up
Say nothing until the full review is complete
Promise that no future harm can occur
Tell the patient that disclosure is unnecessary because the cause is unknown
rationale: When the cause is not yet known, the disclosure discussion should still occur. It should be factual, compassionate, and include a plan to update the patient as more information becomes available.

text: A physician realizes a progress note contains the wrong medication dose. What is the best documentation practice?
options: Add a dated correction or addendum that clearly preserves the original entry
Rewrite the entire chart without marking the change
Ask another clinician to alter it
Leave the error because changing records is always forbidden
rationale: Corrections should be transparent, dated, and clearly identified. The original record should not be hidden or erased.

text: A physician forgot to document a material consent discussion yesterday and remembers it accurately today. What is the best charting approach?
options: Make a clearly labelled, dated late entry describing the discussion
Insert the note as if it was written yesterday
Avoid documenting because it is late
Ask the patient to write the physician's note
Delete unrelated parts of the record to make space
rationale: Late entries should be clearly labelled, dated, and accurate. Records should be maintained in a way that is transparent and consistent with regulatory requirements.

text: A patient asks to access their medical record. There is no identified legal exception or safety concern. What is the best response?
options: Facilitate access according to privacy law and clinic process
Refuse because the physician owns the information
Release only if the patient hires a lawyer
rationale: Patients generally have a right to access their personal health information, subject to identity verification, limited legal exceptions, and appropriate record-access procedures.

text: A physician wants to post a rare case on social media with the patient's age, town, diagnosis, and clinical course but no name. What is the best advice?
options: Do not post identifiable or potentially identifiable patient information without proper consent and safeguards
Post it because the name is removed
Post it only in a private group because screenshots are impossible
Ask followers not to share it
Change one laboratory value and post it
rationale: Removing a name may not de-identify a patient when details are enough for recognition. Social media has privacy, permanence, boundary, and professionalism risks.

text: A patient sends repeated personal messages to their physician's private social media account and asks to meet socially. What is the best response?
options: Maintain professional boundaries, redirect communication to appropriate clinical channels, and document if clinically relevant
Accept because it may improve rapport
Discuss other patients to show trust
Move all care to private messages
rationale: Professional boundaries protect the therapeutic relationship and recognize the power imbalance between physician and patient. Communication should stay within appropriate clinical channels.

text: A close friend asks a physician for controlled medication without a full assessment or record. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Avoid informal prescribing and direct the friend to appropriate clinical care, except for true emergencies or minor limited situations
Ask for payment outside the clinic
rationale: Treating family and friends can impair history, examination, confidentiality, documentation, and objectivity. Informal care is risky and should generally be avoided.

text: A healthy patient with no symptoms asks for a large panel of blood tests because they want to be sure everything is normal. Which response best reflects Canadian resource stewardship?
options: Discuss risks and benefits, avoid tests without a clinical indication, and offer evidence-based screening
Order every test requested to preserve satisfaction
Tell the patient that cost is the only reason to avoid testing
rationale: Choosing Wisely Canada emphasizes conversations that reduce unnecessary tests and treatments because they can expose patients to harm and consume health resources without benefit.

text: A stable inpatient has daily routine bloodwork ordered by habit, with no clinical change and no result expected to affect management. What is the best action?
options: Reassess the indication and stop unnecessary repeat testing
Continue daily tests because routine orders are harmless
Order more tests to avoid missing anything
Tell the patient labs are never harmful
rationale: Unnecessary laboratory testing can cause false positives, anemia from repeated phlebotomy, downstream investigations, and resource strain. Testing should answer a clinical question.

text: A patient with a viral upper respiratory infection requests antibiotics. They have no signs of bacterial infection. Which response is best?
options: Explain why antibiotics are not indicated, discuss expected course and return precautions, and avoid prescribing
Prescribe broad-spectrum antibiotics because they are stronger
Give antibiotics only if the patient promises not to overuse them
rationale: Antibiotic stewardship includes avoiding antibiotics when bacterial infection is not likely, explaining the expected viral course, and giving clear safety-net advice.

text: A patient asks whether a preventive medication is worth taking. The relative risk reduction sounds large, but the absolute baseline risk is low and adverse effects are possible. What is the best counselling approach?
options: Explain absolute benefit, possible harms, alternatives, and the patient's values before deciding together
Use only the relative risk reduction because it sounds clearer
Withhold numbers because patients cannot understand them
Prescribe the medication because prevention is always beneficial
Tell the patient to search online and decide alone
rationale: Ethical counselling requires understandable information. Absolute risk, expected benefit, harms, uncertainty, and patient goals matter more than a persuasive relative-risk number alone.

text: A patient with uncomplicated mechanical low back pain and no red flags requests an MRI because a friend had one. What is the best response?
options: Validate the concern, explain why early imaging is not indicated, discuss red flags and follow-up, and offer evidence-based care
Order CT instead because it is faster
Tell the patient that imaging is denied only because of cost
rationale: Resource stewardship is ethical care. Unnecessary imaging can cause false positives, anxiety, radiation exposure when CT is used, downstream procedures, and system delay for patients who need imaging.

text: An asymptomatic patient asks if they should pay for a private full-body MRI advertised online. They have no risk factors or symptoms. What is the most ethical advice?
options: Discuss uncertain benefit, false positives, overdiagnosis, downstream harm, and evidence-based screening instead
Recommend it because more information is always better
Order extra tumor markers to make the MRI more complete
Say the test is useful only if the patient can afford it
rationale: Ethics includes protecting patients from overdiagnosis and low-value commercial testing. The physician should explain benefit, harm, uncertainty, and appropriate guideline-based screening.

text: A stable outpatient had normal thyroid testing last week. They ask for the same test again today because they feel anxious. What is the best approach?
options: Address the anxiety, explain why repeating the test is unlikely to help, and use retesting only if the clinical picture changes
Repeat the test because it is simple
Tell the patient anxiety is not a medical issue
Document the request but avoid discussion
rationale: Unnecessary repeat testing can lead to false positives and downstream harm. The ethical response combines reassurance, explanation, safety-netting, and appropriate follow-up.

text: A patient with likely viral sinus symptoms wants antibiotics immediately. They are stable and have no red flags. Which plan best supports antimicrobial stewardship?
options: Explain the expected course, provide symptom care and return precautions, and consider delayed prescription only when clinically appropriate
Give broad-spectrum antibiotics today to maintain satisfaction
Order antibiotics without documenting the diagnosis
Tell the patient antibiotics are never harmful
rationale: Antimicrobial stewardship is not just saying no. It includes explanation, symptom treatment, expected duration, red flags, and a plan for reassessment or delayed prescription when suitable.

text: A patient on long-term opioids has repeated early refill requests. The clinician is concerned about harm and possible opioid use disorder. What is the best next step?
options: Reassess pain, function, risks, substance use, and safety; document a clear plan and offer evidence-based support rather than abruptly abandoning the patient
Dismiss the patient immediately from the practice
Increase the dose to avoid conflict
Report the patient to police because early refills prove diversion
rationale: Opioid ethics requires balancing pain care, safety, stigma reduction, documentation, and patient continuity. Concern about misuse should trigger reassessment and support, not abandonment.

text: A clinician plans urine drug screening for a patient receiving chronic opioid therapy. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Explain the purpose, limitations, possible consequences, and how results will be used before testing
Order the test secretly because trust is not needed
Use the result as the only basis for diagnosis
Discharge the patient automatically for any unexpected result
Post the result in a shared waiting-room list
rationale: Monitoring can be clinically appropriate, but it should be transparent and interpreted carefully. Unexpected results require discussion, confirmation when needed, and a patient-safety response.

text: A patient with opioid use disorder misses two appointments and returns asking for help. Which response best reflects ethical care?
options: Use nonjudgmental language, reassess safety and treatment needs, reduce overdose risk, and support re-engagement
Tell the patient they lost the right to care
rationale: Ethical addiction care avoids stigma and focuses on safety, engagement, harm reduction, and evidence-based treatment. Missed appointments are a risk signal, not a reason to abandon care.

text: A specialist has limited appointment slots. A physician asks for an urgent referral mainly because the patient is a personal friend, not because the clinical risk is higher. What is the best ethical principle?
options: Prioritize referrals by clinical urgency and transparent criteria, not personal connection
Upgrade the referral because friendship is relevant
Delay sicker patients to help the friend
Send incomplete information to make the referral look urgent
Ask the patient to exaggerate symptoms
rationale: Fair access means triage based on need, risk, and urgency. Personal relationships should not distort scarce specialist access.

text: A patient needs specialist input. Which referral is most ethical and useful?
options: A clear question, relevant history, prior tests and treatments, urgency, and what the patient understands
A one-line referral saying please assess
A referral marked urgent without clinical reason
A full chart dump with no question
A referral that hides abnormal results
rationale: Good referrals reduce delay, duplication, and harm. The specialist needs a clear clinical question and relevant information, while the patient needs realistic expectations.

text: An older adult with frailty is offered an invasive test that may not change management. What is the best ethical approach?
options: Discuss goals of care, likely benefit, burden, alternatives, and what decision the test would change
Order the test because age must not affect decisions
Withhold all tests because the patient is old
Ask family to decide without the patient
rationale: Frailty should not be used to discriminate. It should guide a goals-based discussion about benefit, burden, function, and patient priorities.

text: A patient leaves visits confused and takes medications incorrectly. What is the best communication strategy?
options: Use plain language, confirm understanding with teach-back, provide reliable patient resources, and adapt the plan
Speak only to family without consent
Stop explaining risks because it takes time
rationale: Valid consent and adherence depend on understanding. Teach-back and reliable patient education reduce harm and respect autonomy.

text: A patient with limited English must consent to surgery. Their child offers to interpret complex risks. What is the best approach?
options: Use a qualified medical interpreter when possible and confirm understanding before consent
Use the child for all details because it is faster
Proceed with consent if the patient nods
Ask the surgeon to sign for the patient
rationale: Language access is an ethics and safety issue. A qualified interpreter supports accurate information, voluntariness, confidentiality, and capacity assessment.

text: A patient does not fill a prescription because of cost but feels embarrassed to say so. What is the most ethical prescribing response?
options: Ask about affordability in a nonjudgmental way and consider effective lower-cost options when clinically appropriate
Keep prescribing the same drug without discussion
Tell the patient cost is outside clinical care
Choose the newest medication for every patient
rationale: Cost affects adherence and outcomes. Ethical prescribing includes discussing affordability, coverage, alternatives, and patient preference without shame.

text: A patient requests treatment for a minor ailment, but the history reveals red flags outside routine management. What is the best professional response?
options: Explain the concern, provide urgent referral or medical assessment as appropriate, and avoid treating beyond safe scope
Prescribe anyway because the patient came for convenience
Ignore red flags if the medication is low risk
Treat first and refer only if treatment fails
Let the patient choose any medication without assessment
rationale: Minor-ailment care requires assessment, recognition of red flags, counselling, and referral when the presentation exceeds safe scope.

text: A capable adolescent requests contraception and asks that parents not be told. There is no abuse concern or other mandatory reporting issue. What is the best response?
options: Assess capacity, provide confidential counselling and care when appropriate, and discuss safety and follow-up
Call the parents after the visit
rationale: Many adolescent sexual health visits test capacity, confidentiality, and safety. Confidential care can be appropriate when the young person is capable and no legal reporting exception applies.

text: A pregnant patient is offered prenatal screening and says they do not know whether they want information that might not change their decision. What is the best response?
options: Explain purpose, possible results, limitations, follow-up options, and respect the patient's informed choice
Order the screen because prenatal testing is routine
Say refusal is unsafe without exploring values
rationale: Screening decisions should be informed and preference-sensitive. The patient needs understandable information about benefit, limits, false positives, and next steps.

text: A patient with obesity avoids care after repeated comments that every symptom is due to weight. What is the best clinician approach?
options: Use respectful language, assess the presenting concern on its own merits, ask permission before weight discussion, and address evidence-based options
Focus only on weight regardless of the complaint
Delay investigation until weight loss occurs
Avoid preventive care because obesity is the main issue
rationale: Weight bias can reduce trust, delay diagnosis, and worsen care. Ethical obesity care is respectful, evidence-based, and patient-centred.

text: A patient says they felt dismissed in a prior visit because of their background and now distrusts the health system. What is the best response?
options: Acknowledge the concern, invite the patient's perspective, address current needs, and use culturally safe, trauma-informed care
Defend the prior clinician before listening
Tell the patient all patients are treated the same
End the visit because trust is low
rationale: Equity questions often test humility, listening, trauma-informed care, and adapting care to the patient rather than assuming equal treatment creates equal outcomes.

text: A patient discloses intimate partner violence but is not ready to leave. They are an adult with capacity and there is no immediate child protection issue disclosed. What is the best next step?
options: Validate, assess immediate danger, offer resources and safety planning, document carefully, and respect the capable patient's choices
Force the patient to leave the relationship today
Call the partner to confirm the story
Ignore the disclosure unless injuries are severe
Postpone all care until police are called
rationale: Ethical IPV care prioritizes safety, autonomy, validation, documentation, and resources. Mandatory reporting depends on jurisdiction and circumstances, especially child risk or imminent danger.

text: A family asks the physician not to tell a capable patient that imaging suggests cancer. The patient asks directly what the scan showed. What is the best response?
options: Explore the family's concern, then answer the capable patient's questions honestly and compassionately
Hide the result because family requested it
Lie and say the scan was normal
Ask family to consent for disclosure
rationale: A capable patient has the right to information about their health. Family concern should be explored, but it does not override the patient's direct request for truthful information.

text: A patient is angry, interrupts repeatedly, and demands a test that is not indicated. Which response is best?
options: Acknowledge emotion, set respectful limits, clarify the clinical concern, explain reasoning, and offer follow-up or reassessment
Order the test only to end the visit
Dismiss the patient immediately without urgent-care coverage
rationale: Professionalism includes de-escalation, boundaries, clear reasoning, and documentation. Anger does not require low-value care or unsafe dismissal.

text: A clinician uses an AI tool that suggests a diagnosis and treatment. The suggestion conflicts with the patient's presentation and local guidance. What is the best ethical approach?
options: Treat AI as support only, verify with clinical judgment and reliable sources, and remain responsible for the decision
Follow the AI because it is faster
Hide AI use in documentation if it affected care
Let the patient decide whether the AI is correct
rationale: AI can support information retrieval, but it does not replace clinical responsibility, local guidance, patient context, or informed consent.

text: A trainee finds conflicting advice on several websites. What is the best approach before applying the advice to a patient?
options: Prefer current, reputable, locally applicable guidance and check whether the recommendation fits the patient
Use only non-Canadian guidance for Canadian exams
Apply a resource even if it is patient education only
rationale: Using online resources ethically means checking credibility, date, jurisdiction, population, conflicts, and whether the source is meant for clinicians or patients.

text: A patient asks for a backdated sick note for days the physician did not assess them and says the employer will not check. What is the best response?
options: Provide only accurate information based on assessment and records, and do not backdate or exaggerate
Backdate it to preserve the relationship
Use vague wording to hide uncertainty
Ask office staff to sign instead
rationale: Medical certificates are professional documents. They should be accurate, limited to necessary information, and based on clinical assessment or reliable record review.

text: A drug company offers to pay for a clinician's travel if the clinician agrees to use the company's product as first choice. What is the best response?
options: Decline arrangements that create a conflict between patient care and personal benefit
Prescribe the product only to patients with insurance
rationale: Conflicts of interest can undermine trust and distort prescribing. Patient welfare and evidence should guide decisions, not personal benefit.

text: During a virtual visit, a patient appears to be in a public place and wants to discuss sensitive results. What is the best first step?
options: Confirm privacy, identity, location, and whether the patient wants to continue before discussing sensitive information
Send the result in an unsecured chat
rationale: Virtual care requires the same consent and privacy principles as in-person care, with extra attention to identity, location, confidentiality, and emergency planning.

sub: Public health restriction and least restrictive care
text: A patient with a reportable infectious disease refuses isolation instructions. Public health law may allow restrictions. Which ethical principle should guide action?
options: Use the least restrictive effective measure, explain the reason, follow legal process, and protect public safety
Use the most restrictive measure first
Ignore the disease because autonomy is absolute
rationale: Public health ethics balances autonomy and community protection. Restrictions should be lawful, necessary, proportionate, and as limited as possible.

text: A rural patient cannot attend repeated urban appointments for screening follow-up. What is the best ethical approach?
options: Explore barriers and coordinate a practical, safe pathway using local or virtual options when appropriate
Tell the patient to move closer
rationale: Equity means adapting care to barriers such as geography, cost, language, disability, and caregiving duties while maintaining safety.

text: A learner is asked to perform a procedure beyond their competence without direct supervision. What is the best response?
options: Pause, disclose learner role as appropriate, obtain consent, and ensure adequate supervision or another qualified clinician
Let the patient assume the learner is fully trained
Document the procedure under the supervisor's name only
rationale: Patients should know relevant learner involvement, and learners must work within competence with supervision. Education never overrides patient safety.

text: A patient has a complication after surgery and asks whether the bad outcome itself proves malpractice. Which set of elements must generally be shown for negligence?
options: Duty of care, breach of the standard of care, harm, and causation
A poor result, patient dissatisfaction, and a written complaint
Any medical error and any later symptom
A signed consent form and an unexpected outcome
rationale: Negligence is not proved by an adverse outcome alone. The usual analysis asks whether there was a duty of care, whether the physician fell below the applicable standard, whether harm occurred, and whether the breach caused the harm.

text: A physician chose a management plan that many competent physicians would have considered reasonable at the time, but the patient later deteriorated. Which statement is most accurate?
options: The standard of care is reasonableness in the circumstances, not perfection or hindsight
Any deterioration proves the standard of care was breached
The best specialist opinion after the event always defines negligence
A physician is liable whenever another option existed
Only written guidelines define the legal standard of care
rationale: The standard of care asks what a reasonable physician would have done with the information available at the time. Guidelines help, but they do not automatically replace clinical judgment or create perfection as the standard.

text: A capable patient refuses pelvic examination. The clinician performs it anyway because it is clinically important. Which medico-legal concept is most directly engaged?
options: Battery because physical contact occurred without valid consent
Defamation because the patient was offended
Negligence only if the examination was painful
Fraud only if the chart was altered
rationale: Touching a patient for an examination or treatment without valid consent can constitute battery even if the clinician believes the examination is medically useful.

text: At a community event, a physician gives a detailed individualized medical opinion to a person who then relies on it. Which risk is most important?
options: A duty of care may be created when individualized advice is given and relied on
No duty can ever arise outside a clinic
The advice is protected because no chart exists
The person must pay a fee before any duty exists
